title: At your service
paragraphs: Hey, welcome to Swallowtail, an automation toolkit for Godot. Let's make a few changes to this stretch of coast. I'll show you how to connect the editor, automate a workflow, and bring an AI agent into the process.
text: Hey, welcome to Swallowtail, an automation toolkit for Godot. Let's make a few changes to this stretch of coast. I'll show you how to connect the editor, automate a workflow, and bring an AI agent into the process.

title: Why not just use the editor?
paragraphs: Before we start, there's an obvious question: why not just use the editor? If I'm moving one rock, I probably would. It's easy to place it by eye. Swallowtail becomes useful when I want to repeat that work, try several variations, or let an agent help with the changes.
Godot's own command line already handles imports, scripts, and exports. Swallowtail also lets us reach into the editor we're working in. Let's connect it.

title: Connect the editor
paragraphs: With Godot and the Swallowtail binary installed, I'll open a terminal in the project folder. From here, I can install and enable the addon, then launch the editor. The status command tells me whether the connection is ready.
Whenever I need an option, I can ask for help. Here, node set explains how to change a property. Next, I'll read the scene tree to find our lighthouse.

title: Shape the shoreline
paragraphs: The shoreline could use another rock. I'll duplicate this one, name the copy, and bring it closer to shore. A small change to its scale helps it fit.

title: When the work scales up
paragraphs: So far, these are small edits. But imagine adjusting hundreds of rocks, or comparing five versions of this coast with different water and lighting. That's when a repeatable set of commands starts to save work. I can choose the settings once and apply them again.
You could write a Godot script for that, too. Swallowtail gives you ready-made commands to build on, whether you're writing the automation yourself or asking an agent to help.

title: What the AI actually does
paragraphs: I can ask an AI agent to keep the calmer water, lower the sun, and warm the light, then save the scene for review. Here's the workflow: inspect the project, look up the commands, apply the changes, and read the results back.

The agent gets feedback from Godot as it works, and I can check both the commands and the scene. If something isn't right, I can adjust it or ask for another pass. I still decide how this coast should look.

title: Where MCP fits
paragraphs: An agent with terminal access can use those same CLI commands. MCP, or Model Context Protocol, gives AI clients another way to discover and call Swallowtail's tools. Both routes reach the same operations in Godot.
Here, the client connects to Swallowtail through standard input and output. It calls a tool to lower the sun, and we can watch the scene change.
Then it reads the sun's rotation back, so we can check that the change took effect.

title: Choose your workflow
paragraphs: You can use Swallowtail yourself, reuse your commands in scripts, or connect an agent when it helps. AI and MCP are optional. And throughout that workflow, you're working with ordinary Godot scenes and scripts.
